lines.text: A tiny island at the crossroads of the Mediterranean, with temples older than the pyramids. This is the story of Malta, from its first builders to today.
About six thousand years ago, Malta's first farmers began carving a vast underground burial place into the rock.
Soon they raised great stone temples on the surface too, standing long before the pyramids of Egypt.
Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs and Normans followed. Far away in Jerusalem, a hospital for pilgrims gave rise to the Knights of St John.
Driven from Rhodes, the Knights came to Malta in 1530. In 1565 a huge Ottoman army besieged them, and the Knights held out.
The next year they began building a new fortified capital, Valletta, named after their Grand Master.
In 1571 Caravaggio was born, the painter who, fleeing Rome after a killing, would find shelter for a time among the Knights.
In Valletta they built St John's, their great church, where Caravaggio's Beheading of Saint John still hangs.
In 1798 Napoleon seized Malta on his way to Egypt, ending the Knights' rule. The French stayed just two years.
Then the British came, and from 1813 Malta was a Crown Colony and a great naval base.
In 1916 Dom Mintoff was born, the prime minister who would make Malta a republic.
In the Second World War, Malta was bombed again and again for two years, and the whole island was given the George Cross.
In 1964 Daphne Caruana Galizia was born, the journalist whose murder by car bomb in 2017 shook the nation.
That same year, Malta became independent from Britain, and ten years later a republic.
In 1977 Robert Abela was born, who became prime minister in 2020.
And in 2004, Malta joined the European Union, one of ten countries to join together.
Small as it is, Malta has stood at the centre of the Mediterranean for six thousand years.
